title: Conductors and insulators: what lets electricity through, what holds it back, and why the answer can change

summary.text: A steel spoon lights the bulb and a plastic ruler does not. But is a cup of water a conductor or an insulator? In this lesson you build two testers, a bulb and a small red light called an LED, and you find that they do not always agree. You learn what moves inside a wire and inside salt water, why your own body conducts, and why every plug, wire and switch is made of a conductor wrapped in an insulator. You also meet the things that sit in between, such as pencil lead, the chips in a phone, and the air that lightning breaks through.
summary.art: A table with two small testers side by side: one with a dark torch bulb and one with a glowing red LED, both with their wire ends dipped in the same plastic cup of water.

intro.hook: Look at any wire at home, without touching the socket. On the outside there is plastic. Inside there is metal. Every wire in every home in the world is made this way, from Kochi to Kohima. Why two materials? And here is a harder one: water is not a metal, so why does everyone say never to touch a switch with wet hands?
intro.text: Some materials let electricity through easily. We call them conductors. Some hold it back so well that almost nothing gets through. We call them insulators. In this lesson you test water, salt, sugar, lemon, a pencil, a tomato and your own fingertip, using only AA cells. You find out what is really moving inside each one. You read a plug as a map of conductors and insulators, and you learn the reason behind each safety rule. Then you look again at the two boxes, conductor and insulator, and ask whether the world really comes in two boxes at all.
intro.art: A cut-open electric wire drawn large: shiny copper strands in the middle, a coloured plastic coat around them, and a child's finger pointing at the place where the two meet.

outcomes: I can build a circuit tester and use it in a fair test to rank materials by how well they conduct.
I can explain why metals and graphite conduct, and why plastic, rubber, dry wood and glass insulate, by saying which have charges that are free to move.
I can explain why tap water and salt water conduct, why very pure water hardly conducts, and what ions are.
I can explain why my body conducts, and why 230 volts with wet hands is dangerous when a 1.5 volt cell is not.
I can point to the conductors and the insulators in a plug, a wire, a switch and a torch, and say why each one is where it is.
I can explain why conductor and insulator are two ends of one long scale, and give examples that sit in between or change.
I can give the safety rules for electricity at home, with the reason for each one.
I can say what is still argued about or not yet known, and give two views fairly.

terms.meaning: A material that lets electric charge move through it easily.
terms.example: The copper inside a wire and the steel of a spoon are conductors.
terms.art: A steel spoon joining two wires, with a torch bulb glowing brightly beside it.

terms.meaning: A material that holds electric charge back so strongly that almost none gets through.
terms.example: The plastic coat on a wire is an insulator. It keeps the electricity in the copper and away from your hand.
terms.art: A plastic ruler joining two wires, with a dark torch bulb beside it.

terms.meaning: A very tiny particle with an electric charge. Every atom has electrons. In a metal, some of them are free to move from atom to atom.
terms.example: When you close a torch switch, the free electrons all along the wire start to drift together.
terms.art: A zoom-in on a metal wire showing rows of atoms with small dots moving freely between them.

terms.meaning: An atom, or a small group of atoms, that carries an electric charge. Ions can move through water.
terms.example: Salt in water breaks into sodium ions and chloride ions. They carry the electricity through salt water.
terms.art: A zoom-in on a cup of salt water showing two kinds of small balls, marked plus and minus, drifting in opposite directions between two wires.

terms.meaning: A flow of electric charge. In a wire the moving charges are electrons. In water they are ions.
terms.example: A bigger current makes a bulb glow brighter.
terms.art: A loop of wire with a cell and a bulb, and arrows showing a flow going all the way round.

terms.meaning: How strongly a thing holds back the current. A good conductor has a small resistance. An insulator has a huge one.
terms.example: A long pencil lead has more resistance than a steel spoon, so the bulb glows dimmer with the pencil.
terms.art: Two pipes side by side, one wide and one narrow, with more water coming out of the wide one.

terms.meaning: A circuit with one gap in it. You put a thing across the gap. If the lamp lights, the thing has let current through.
terms.example: Your bulb tester has two cells, a bulb and two free wire ends.
terms.art: A cell holder, a bulb in a holder and three wires, with two free ends held just apart.

terms.meaning: A small lamp made from a semiconductor. An LED lights with a far smaller current than a torch bulb needs, and only one way round.
terms.example: A red LED glows through a cup of tap water. A torch bulb stays dark.
terms.art: A small red LED with one long leg and one short leg, glowing.

terms.meaning: Volts measure how hard a cell or a socket pushes the charges. More volts means a harder push.
terms.example: One AA cell pushes with 1.5 volts. A wall socket in India pushes with 230 volts.
terms.art: A small AA cell marked 1.5 V next to a wall socket marked 230 V, with a small arrow and a very large arrow.

terms.meaning: The electricity that comes to a home through wires from a power station. In India it pushes with 230 volts, which can kill.
terms.example: Fans, fridges and wet grinders run on mains electricity. Experiments never do.
terms.art: A power line running from a pole to a house, with a fan and a fridge inside.

terms.meaning: What happens when an electric current passes through a body. A big enough current can burn the body and stop the heart.
terms.example: A cracked plug can give a shock, because the insulator no longer covers the metal.
terms.art: A cracked plug with a red warning mark over the bare metal inside.

terms.meaning: A wire that joins the metal body of an appliance to the ground. If a fault makes the body live, the current takes the earth wire.
terms.example: The thick top pin of a three-pin plug is the earth pin.
terms.art: A three-pin plug with the thick top pin coloured green, and a green wire running from it down into the ground.

terms.meaning: A material that conducts a little, and whose conducting can be changed by heat, light, a push or tiny amounts of other atoms.
terms.example: Silicon is a semiconductor. The chips in a phone and the cells in a solar panel are made of it.
terms.art: A grey computer chip beside a blue solar panel and a red LED.

terms.meaning: A material that, when made cold enough, has no resistance at all.
terms.example: The magnets inside a hospital MRI scanner are coils of superconducting wire kept very cold.
terms.art: A small magnet floating above a dark disc in a dish of misty, very cold liquid.

explanations.concept: Conductors and insulators: are the charges free to move?
explanations.context: This card says what a conductor and an insulator are. It comes first because every other card builds on it.
explanations.definition: A conductor is a material in which electric charges can move easily. An insulator is a material in which the charges are held so firmly that almost none can move.
explanations.description: Every material is made of atoms, and every atom holds charged particles. So every material is full of charge. What differs is whether any of that charge is free to move. In copper, some electrons are free and drift along when a cell pushes them. In plastic, every electron is held by its own atom. A push of 3 volts moves almost none of them. That is why a spoon across the gap of a tester lights the bulb and a ruler does not. Here is what we know so far, said honestly: no material is a perfect insulator. With a hard enough push, a little charge moves in anything.
examples: Conductors: copper, aluminium, steel, iron, silver, gold, and graphite, which is the dark part of a pencil.
Insulators: plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood, dry cloth, dry paper, wax and dry air.
Copper lets charge through more than a million million million times more easily than glass does.

perspectives.explanation: Sort every material into two boxes, conductor or insulator. This is quick and it keeps people safe. An electrician needs to know at once what she may touch.

There are no two boxes. There is one long scale of resistance, from silver at one end to rubber and glass at the other. Sea water, pencil lead, silicon, wet wood and skin all sit somewhere along the scale. Where we draw the line depends on the job.

perspectives.who: William Gilbert, a doctor in London, in 1600
perspectives.explanation: He also made two boxes, but different ones. Things that pulled dust when rubbed, such as amber and glass, he called electrics. Metals did not, so people thought metals had no electricity in them. Today we know metals are full of free charge.

explanations.art: A long horizontal scale drawn like a ruler. At the far left a silver ring and a copper wire, then a steel spoon, a pencil, a cup of sea water, a cup of tap water, a wet stick, a fingertip, a dry stick, and at the far right a rubber glove and a glass marble.

explanations.concept: Why metals conduct: electrons that belong to the whole piece
explanations.context: This card looks inside a metal. It is here because the tester only shows that a spoon conducts, and this card says why.
explanations.definition: In a metal, each atom lets go of one or more of its outer electrons. These free electrons belong to the whole piece of metal and can move through it.
explanations.description: A copper wire is already full of free electrons before you join it to anything. The cell does not pour electrons into the wire. The cell pushes the ones that are already there, all at once, all round the loop. Each electron drifts slowly, less than a millimetre each second. But all of them start together, so the bulb lights at once. In plastic and rubber the electrons are locked into the bonds between atoms. Graphite is a surprise. Graphite is pure carbon, not a metal, yet each carbon atom has one electron free to move along its flat sheet. Diamond is pure carbon too, with every electron locked, and diamond is an insulator.
examples: A line of coins on a table, pushed at one end: the last coin moves at once, though each coin moves only a little.
A pencil lead conducts. A diamond made of the same carbon atoms does not.
Metals that conduct electricity well also conduct heat well, because the same free electrons carry both.

perspectives.who: Paul Drude, a physicist in Germany, in 1900
perspectives.explanation: The free electrons are like a gas of tiny balls flying about between the atoms. A push makes the whole gas drift. This picture is simple, and it gives the right answer for many metals.

perspectives.who: Felix Bloch in 1928 and Alan Wilson in 1931
perspectives.explanation: Electrons are not tiny balls. They behave as waves spread through the whole crystal, and only some energies are allowed, in bands. A metal has a band that is partly full, so its electrons can move. An insulator has full bands and a wide gap. This picture also explains semiconductors, which the gas picture cannot.

explanations.art: Two zoom-in circles. In the first, labelled copper, rows of atoms with loose dots drifting between them. In the second, labelled plastic, atoms joined in chains with every dot held between two atoms.

explanations.concept: Does water conduct? The ions do the carrying
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Water Test. It is here because water has no free electrons, yet the LED glowed.
explanations.definition: Water conducts when it holds ions, which are charged atoms from dissolved salts, minerals or acids. The ions move through the water and carry the current.
explanations.description: Water has no free electrons the way a metal has. Very pure water is a poor conductor. But water is very good at pulling salts apart into ions. Table salt in water splits into sodium ions with a plus charge and chloride ions with a minus charge. Put two wires in, and the plus ions drift one way and the minus ions drift the other. That movement is the current. More ions means more current, so each pinch of salt makes the LED brighter. Tap water has minerals from rock and soil, so it conducts a little. Sugar dissolves just as well as salt, but sugar stays as whole molecules with no charge, so it adds nothing. The water inside your body, in rivers, in the sea and on a wet bathroom floor is full of ions.
examples: A red LED glows faintly through tap water and brightly through salt water.
Sea water conducts about a million times better than the purest water a laboratory can make.
The small meter that a water-filter technician dips in your drinking water is a conductivity tester. It counts dissolved minerals by how well the water conducts.

perspectives.explanation: Water conducts electricity. Treat every drop as a conductor. For the water we meet in daily life this is the right rule, because that water always holds ions, and 230 volts pushes hard.

perspectives.who: Chemists, after Svante Arrhenius in 1884 and Friedrich Kohlrausch in 1894
perspectives.explanation: Water itself is almost an insulator. The dissolved ions do the carrying. Kohlrausch made water purer than anyone had before and found that it conducted very little, though never zero. A few water molecules always split into ions by themselves.

perspectives.who: Sharks, rays and other fishes of the sea
perspectives.explanation: Sea water is a conductor that carries news. Adrianus Kalmijn showed in 1971 that sharks find a hidden flatfish by the tiny electric signals her body sends through the water. For a shark, conducting water is a sense to hunt with.

explanations.art: Three cups in a row with two wires in each. In the first, labelled pure water, only water molecules. In the second, labelled sugar water, whole sugar molecules with no charge marks. In the third, labelled salt water, plus and minus balls drifting to opposite wires, and a glowing LED above it.

explanations.concept: Your body conducts: why 230 volts and wet hands do not mix
explanations.context: This card is about your own body as a conductor. It is here because it gives the reason behind the safety rules.
explanations.definition: An electric shock is a current passing through a body. The body conducts because the water in every cell is full of ions.
explanations.description: Your body is more than half water, and that water is salty. Blood, sweat and tears all conduct. Dry skin is the body's own insulator. From hand to hand through dry skin, the resistance is about 100,000 ohms or more. Ohms are how resistance is counted. Wet skin can be 100 times easier to get through. A 1.5 volt cell pushes too gently to send a current you could notice through skin, wet or dry. A wall socket pushes with 230 volts, more than 150 times as hard. Through wet skin that is enough to stop a heart, because the heart beats on small electric signals of its own. So the rule is not that water is dangerous and dry is safe. Mains electricity is dangerous always. Water takes away the little protection that dry skin gives.
examples: Dry hands before touching any switch. Never use a hair dryer, phone charger or heater in a wet bathroom.
A bird sits safely on one bare power line, because both feet are on the same wire and no current is pushed through her body.
A phone screen works because your fingertip conducts. A thick glove on the finger does nothing.
explanations.one_view: Doctors and safety engineers have measured this many times, and all agree that a mains current through the chest can kill, so there is no honest second view to give a child here.
explanations.art: A child's outline with the inside tinted blue to show salty water, a thin dry layer of skin drawn as a dotted line, and a small 1.5 V cell on one side and a 230 V socket with a red cross on the other.

explanations.concept: Conductors and insulators working as a team in every appliance
explanations.context: This card shows how plugs, wires and switches are built. It is here so you can read any appliance as a map of conductors and insulators.
explanations.definition: An electrical appliance uses conductors to lead the current where it is wanted, and insulators to keep it away from everywhere else, above all from people.
explanations.description: Look at a plug that is out of the socket. The pins are brass, a conductor, because they must carry current in. The body is hard plastic, an insulator, because fingers hold it. Inside the cord are three copper wires, each in a plastic coat of a different colour, so the three never touch each other. A switch is a small metal bridge inside a plastic box. Press it, and the bridge closes the gap. An electric iron has a metal plate that must get hot, and a plastic handle that must not carry heat or current. The metal body of a mixer, a fridge or a wet grinder is joined to the earth wire. If a wire inside comes loose and touches the body, the current runs down the earth wire into the ground. That is a far easier path than a person. The big current trips a safety switch at the meter board.
examples: Power lines across the country are bare aluminium, held away from the steel towers by stacks of ceramic or glass discs. The air around them is the insulator.
A line worker wears thick rubber gloves and uses tools with rubber handles.
Inside an electric iron, thin sheets of mica, a mineral mined in Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh, keep the hot wire from touching the metal plate.
explanations.one_view: This is how appliances are built, and anyone can check it by looking at a plug or opening a torch, so there is only the one honest account.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a three-pin plug and cord: brass pins, three copper wires in red, black and green coats, and the plastic body around them, with conductors tinted warm orange and insulators tinted cool blue.

explanations.concept: In between, and both: graphite, semiconductors and insulators that give way
explanations.context: This card looks at the things that will not stay in one box. It is here because your two testers disagreed, and this explains how that can be.
explanations.definition: A semiconductor is a material that conducts a little, and whose conducting changes a great deal with heat, light, the size of the push, or a few added atoms.
explanations.description: Whether a thing conducts depends on more than what it is made of. It depends on the push. Dry air is a very good insulator, yet a push of about 30,000 volts across one centimetre tears electrons off the air's atoms. Then the air conducts, and we see a spark. Lightning is the same thing across a kilometre of sky. It depends on heat. Cold glass insulates. Red-hot glass conducts. It depends on water. Dry wood insulates, and a wet tree carries lightning to the ground. It depends on light. A solar panel conducts better when the Sun shines on it. And it depends on the tester. A torch bulb needs a large current to glow, so the bulb reports salt water as an insulator. An LED needs very little, so the LED reports it as a conductor. Silicon sits in the middle of the scale. By adding a few other atoms, engineers make it conduct exactly when they want. Every chip in a phone is billions of tiny silicon switches.
examples: A red LED is itself a semiconductor. It conducts one way round and not the other.
In Kolkata in 1901, Jagadish Chandra Bose used a crystal of galena, a semiconductor, to detect radio waves. His American patent was granted in 1904.
A pencil line on paper conducts a little. A thicker, darker, shorter line conducts more.

perspectives.explanation: Each material has one right box. Graphite is a conductor, air is an insulator. This is true for a small push at room temperature, which is the only test most classrooms can do.

Conducting is not a fixed label on a material. It is how the material answers a question we put to it, and the answer changes with the push, the heat, the light, the wetness and the purity. One sheet of graphite, called graphene, is among the best conductors known. A stack of such sheets pressed with clay is a pencil lead.

explanations.art: Four small scenes in a row: a lightning bolt through air, a glass rod glowing red-hot between two wires with a lit bulb, a wet tree in rain, and a solar panel in sunlight, each with a small label saying what changed.

explanations.concept: Superconductors: when resistance drops to nothing
explanations.context: This card is about the far end of the scale, beyond the best ordinary conductor. It is here because nobody has yet fully explained it.
explanations.definition: A superconductor is a material that carries a current with no resistance at all, once it is colder than its own special temperature.
explanations.description: Even copper wastes some energy as heat. In 1911 in Leiden, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes and his team cooled mercury to minus 269 degrees Celsius. Its resistance did not just get small. It dropped to nothing. A current started in a ring of superconductor has been watched for months and has not weakened. In 1986 Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller found that some ceramics superconduct at much higher temperatures. Ceramics are usually insulators, so this was a great surprise. Within months, a team led by Maw-Kuen Wu and Paul Chu found one that works at minus 180 degrees, which cheap liquid nitrogen can reach. Scientists agree on how the cold metals do it. They do not agree on how the ceramics do it.
examples: The magnets in hospital MRI scanners are superconducting coils cooled with liquid helium.
A small magnet floats above a superconductor cooled in liquid nitrogen.
If wires could superconduct at room temperature, almost no electricity would be lost between a power station and a home.

perspectives.who: John Bardeen, Leon Cooper and Robert Schrieffer, in 1957
perspectives.explanation: In a cold metal the electrons join into pairs, helped by tiny shakes of the atoms around them. The pairs all move as one and nothing can slow just one of them. This theory fits the cold metals very well and won a Nobel Prize.

perspectives.who: Philip Anderson, a physicist at Princeton, from 1987
perspectives.explanation: In the ceramics the pairs do not need the shaking atoms. The pairing comes from the electrons' own magnetism, in a new state of matter. He argued this until his death in 2020.

perspectives.who: Douglas Scalapino, David Pines and others
perspectives.explanation: The pairs in the ceramics are glued by waves of magnetism that pass between the electrons. This is not the same as Anderson's idea, and experiments have not yet settled between them.

explanations.art: A graph drawn by hand: resistance on the side, coldness along the bottom, and a line that slopes gently down and then falls straight to zero, with a small floating magnet drawn at the zero end.

explanations.concept: Living conductors: nerves, electric senses and signalling plants
explanations.context: This card looks at how living beings use conductors and insulators inside their own bodies. It is here because life found these ideas long before any wire was made.
explanations.definition: Living cells carry electric signals by moving ions through the salty water inside and around them, and they use fatty layers as insulators.
explanations.description: Every living cell is wrapped in a skin of fat only two molecules thick. Fat is an insulator. In that skin are tiny gates that open and shut to let ions through. So every cell is a small bag of conducting water inside an insulating coat with switches in it. A nerve is a long cell who passes a signal along by opening gate after gate. Many nerves are wrapped in extra layers of a fatty insulator called myelin, much like the plastic on a wire. With that wrap a signal can travel about 100 metres in a second. Plants carry electric signals too. Jagadish Chandra Bose measured them in Kolkata more than a hundred years ago. A touch-me-not folds her leaves after an electric signal runs down the stalk. Plants sense, signal and decide. Some scientists call these automatic responses.
examples: Bumblebees can sense the weak electric charge on a flower, and learn from that charge which flowers to visit (Dominic Clarke and others, 2013).
An electric eel stacks thousands of flat cells in a row to make a push of up to 860 volts.
A Venus flytrap shuts after two touches close together, each touch sending an electric signal.

perspectives.who: František Baluška, Stefano Mancuso and others, from 2006
perspectives.explanation: Plants pass electric signals from cell to cell, weigh many signals and choose what to do. This is so like what nerves do that the study deserves the name plant neurobiology, and the activity deserves the name thinking.

perspectives.who: Amedeo Alpi and 35 other plant scientists, in 2007, and Lincoln Taiz in 2019
perspectives.explanation: Plants do signal with electricity, and that is wonderful enough. But the signals do not run through nerve cells or meet in one gathering place, so words such as nerve and mind mislead. The signals are better understood as chemistry and growth.

perspectives.who: Michael Levin, a biologist at Tufts University
perspectives.explanation: All cells, not only nerves, talk to each other with patterns of voltage. In his laboratory, changing these patterns made flatworms grow a head at each end. He argues that bodies use electricity to remember and decide what shape to be.

explanations.art: A nerve fibre drawn like a wire with fatty beads of insulation along it, next to a real wire with a plastic coat, and below them a touch-me-not with folded leaves and a small wavy signal line running down the stalk.

agreed.text: Copper and glass differ in how easily charge moves through them by more than a million million million times. No other everyday property of materials has so wide a range.
agreed.evidence: Laboratories measure the resistance of a bar of each material with meters. The numbers have been checked for more than a century and are printed in standard tables.

agreed.text: When a current passes through salt water, new substances collect at the two wires. This shows that matter itself, the ions, is moving through the water.
agreed.evidence: Michael Faraday measured this in London in 1834 and gave us the word ion. You can see small bubbles form on the wire ends in the Water Test.

agreed.text: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. One is an insulator and the other a conductor, so the way atoms are joined matters as much as which atoms they are.
agreed.evidence: In 1797 Smithson Tennant burned a diamond and got exactly the same gas, in the same amount, as from burning the same weight of charcoal.

agreed.text: Wet skin lets through about 100 times more current than dry skin does, for the same push.
agreed.evidence: Safety engineers measured the resistance of many people's bodies, dry and wet. The results are the basis of the world standard on electric shock, IEC 60479.

agreed.text: A current in a ring of superconductor does not fade.
agreed.evidence: In 1963 J. File and R. G. Mills watched such a current closely. From the tiny change they could measure, they worked out that the current would last at least 100,000 years.

challenging.claim: Electricity always takes the path of least resistance.
challenging.who: A very common saying, also heard from some electricians.
challenging.for: When there are two paths, most of the current does go through the easier one. This is why an earth wire protects a person.
challenging.against: Current takes every path open to it at once, and shares itself out. The easier path gets more, but the harder path still gets some. A person touching a live wire gets a shock even when an easier path exists nearby.
challenging.context: This card tests a saying that sounds right. It is here because the true version explains why an earth wire helps but is never a reason to be careless.

challenging.claim: Pure water does not conduct electricity at all.
challenging.who: Many books that correct the saying that water is a conductor.
challenging.for: Very pure water conducts about a million times worse than sea water. In a classroom test with a bulb, it looks like a perfect insulator.
challenging.against: Friedrich Kohlrausch and Adolf Heydweiller measured the purest water they could make in 1894. It still conducted a little. About two water molecules in every thousand million split into ions by themselves. And pure water does not stay pure. It takes in gas from the air and salts from any cup or hand within minutes.
challenging.context: This card looks at a correction that goes too far. It is here so that the lesson does not swap one half-truth for another.

challenging.claim: Rubber chappals or rubber tyres keep a person safe from electric shock and lightning.
challenging.who: A belief held by many people in many countries.
challenging.for: Rubber is a very good insulator. Line workers do wear rubber gloves and boots, tested for the job.
challenging.against: A chappal sole is thin, often wet and dirty, and not made or tested for 230 volts. Lightning has just crossed a kilometre of air, so a centimetre of rubber is nothing to it. A car is fairly safe in a storm because of the metal body, which leads the current round the people inside.
challenging.context: This card looks at a belief about rubber. It is here because it mixes a true fact with a dangerous conclusion.

challenging.claim: A material can be made that superconducts at room temperature and ordinary pressure.
challenging.who: Many physicists. Vitaly Ginzburg, who won a Nobel Prize in 2003, argued for decades that no law of nature forbids it.
challenging.for: The record temperature keeps rising. In 2019 two teams, one including Maddury Somayazulu, found a compound of lanthanum and hydrogen that superconducts at about minus 23 degrees Celsius, though only when squeezed harder than the deepest rock inside the Earth.
challenging.against: Every claim for room temperature so far has failed when other laboratories checked it. A paper from 2020 was withdrawn in 2022. A material called LK-99, announced in 2023, turned out not to superconduct. Some physicists think the atoms cannot hold electron pairs together when they are that warm, without huge pressure.
challenging.context: This card is about a search going on now. It is here because it shows scientists disagreeing, checking each other, and not yet knowing.

challenging.claim: Electric signals between ordinary cells, not only nerves, store memories and make decisions about the shape of a body.
challenging.who: Michael Levin and his laboratory at Tufts University.
challenging.for: Changing the voltage pattern in a cut flatworm made her grow two heads, and the change lasted when she was cut again, with no change to her genes (Durant and others, 2017). Changing voltage in a tadpole's body made an eye grow on the gut (Pai and others, 2012).
challenging.against: Many biologists say the voltage is one signal among many, switched on by genes and chemicals, and that words like memory and decision claim too much. The work has been done in a few kinds of animals so far.
challenging.context: This card is about a new idea on what electricity does in living bodies. It is here because it asks whether conducting and deciding are linked far more widely than in brains.

big_questions.q: The bulb said salt water is an insulator. The LED said it is a conductor. Which tester told the truth?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each tester needs before it can glow. Is a tester's answer about the water, or about the water and the tester together?

big_questions.q: If no material is a perfect insulator and none is a perfect conductor at room temperature, why do we keep the two words?
big_questions.hint: Think about who uses the words, and for what job. When is a rough word more useful than an exact number?

big_questions.q: Diamond and pencil lead are made of the same atoms. So where does being a conductor come from?
big_questions.hint: Think of the same bricks built into a wall and into a bridge. What is different, if not the bricks?

big_questions.q: A wire is copper wrapped in plastic. A nerve is salty water wrapped in fat. Did humans invent the wire, or copy it?
big_questions.hint: Think about which came first, and whether an inventor has to know that she is copying.

big_questions.q: Your skin is the line where the conducting inside of you meets the insulating air. Is that line where you end?
big_questions.hint: Think about a phone screen that senses your finger, a shark who senses a hidden swimmer through water, and a hand held near a hot tawa.

big_questions.q: The same rule about water, ions and danger is true in every home on Earth. Yet safe wiring and earthing are not in every home. Why not?
big_questions.hint: Think about who builds houses, who checks them, what it costs, and who is asked.

big_questions.q: Is there anything in the world that belongs fully in one box, with no in-between?
big_questions.hint: Try some pairs: hot and cold, alive and not alive, tall and short, day and night. Look for where the line would go.

story.title: The Tingle in the Grinder
text: It had rained on Thanjavur for three days. In the last house on the lane, the wall behind the kitchen shelf had grown a dark damp patch.
Imran, who was eight, was helping his grandfather grind the batter for tomorrow's idlis. Nana poured the soaked rice into the wet grinder. Imran put his palm on the steel drum to feel it hum.
He pulled his hand back fast. "Nana! It bit me!" It was not quite pain. It was a buzzing tingle, like ants running up his fingers.
Nana dried his hands on his towel and turned the grinder off at the wall switch. "Nobody touches it," he said. "Go and call Vasuki."
Vasuki was the electrician who lived three doors down. Her niece Ilakkiya, who was ten, spent every holiday carrying her tool bag. The two of them came through the rain under one umbrella.

Vasuki did not go to the grinder. She went to the meter board by the front door and pushed the main switch down. The fan above them slowed and stopped. "Now the whole house is asleep," she said. "Now we can look."
She pulled out the grinder's plug and held it up. It had two pins. "Where is the third?"
Nana looked at his feet. "The old plug broke. The shop had only this kind."

Ilakkiya put the plug in Imran's hand. "Three wires should come out of a grinder," she said. "Two carry the current in and out. The third is joined to the steel drum. It goes to the thick top pin, and from there down a wire into the ground under the house. It does nothing at all, every day, for years. It waits."
"Waits for what?"
"For today."

Vasuki opened the base of the grinder. Rainwater from the damp wall had crept along the cord. Where the cord bent, the old plastic coat had cracked, and a hair of copper showed through. The copper touched nothing. But it was wet, and the wet ran on to the steel drum.
"But water is not metal," said Imran.
Ilakkiya had been hoping he would say that. From the tool bag she took two small cells, a red LED no bigger than a lentil, and two wires. "Bring me a tumbler of drinking water and the salt."

She dipped the two wire ends into the water. The LED showed the faintest red. Imran had to cup his hands around it to see. "Now one pinch," she said. He dropped it in. The red grew. "One more." Now it shone like a dot of kumkum.

"The water is not the wire," said Ilakkiya. "The salt is. Bits of salt too small to see, each one carrying a charge, swimming from one wire to the other. Water that has run down a wall has picked up salts from the bricks. And now lick the back of your hand."
Imran licked it. "Salty."
"You are a tumbler of salt water with a skin on."
Imran thought about that. "So the electricity went from the cracked wire to the water, from the water to the drum, from the drum to me. And then where?"

"Through you. Out through your feet, into the damp floor, into the ground, and back along the ground to the big grey transformer at the end of the street. For half a second you were a piece of the circuit."
Imran looked at his hand as if it belonged to somebody else. "Why was it only a tingle?"

Vasuki answered without looking up. "Your feet were on Nana's rubber mat. The wet path was long and thin. Your hand was dry. Each of those held back most of the current. Most, not all. That was luck, and I do not like luck."

She cut away the cracked length of cord and fitted a plug with three pins. She tested the socket to make sure its earth wire truly reached the ground. Only then did she push the main switch up. The fan began to turn.
She held a small screwdriver with a tiny lamp in its handle against the steel drum. The lamp stayed dark. "An hour ago it would have glowed," she said.

Ilakkiya leaned close to Imran. "That tester glows only when a tiny current goes through Chithi herself. In through the tip, out through her thumb on the metal cap. It is far too small to notice. She is part of the circuit on purpose."
"On purpose?"
"Inside the handle is a part that holds back almost all of the current. Almost all. Nothing holds back all of it."

That night the idlis were soft, and Nana gave Ilakkiya four. Imran lay awake afterwards, following the path in his head. The cracked wire, the water, the drum, his hand, his feet, the floor, the ground, the street. He had always thought of his skin as the edge of himself, where he stopped and the world began. Today, for half a second, electricity had not seen an edge there at all. He wondered where else his edge was not really an edge.
story.epiphany: Water carries a current because of the ions dissolved in it, and a body is salty water inside a thin skin. An insulator holds back almost all of the current and never quite all, so safety comes from keeping every insulator whole and dry, and from giving the current a far easier path to the ground.
ask: An earth wire can do nothing for years. What is it for, and how would you know if yours was missing?
A tiny current is safe and a larger one can kill. Who should decide how small is small enough, and how could they find out?
Where does a circuit end: at the plug, at the wall, at the transformer in the street, or somewhere else?
art: A kitchen in an old Thanjavur house in the rains: a steel wet grinder on the floor on a rubber mat, a damp patch on the wall behind it, a boy pulling his hand back and a grandfather with a towel on his shoulder.
A woman electrician in a raincoat holding up a two-pin plug by the open front door, with a girl beside her carrying a canvas tool bag and a meter board on the wall with the main switch down.
A girl and a boy crouched over a steel tumbler of water with two wire ends in it, a tiny red LED glowing, and a pinch of salt falling from the boy's fingers.
A boy lying awake at night, with a soft dotted line drawn from a grinder through his hand and feet, down into the ground and along to a transformer on a pole at the end of the lane.
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real. Only a trained electrician tests house wiring. If any appliance gives a tingle, switch off at the main switch and call one.

games.title: Safe Cable: a card game of conductors, insulators and it depends
games.context: This is a card game. You collect conductor cards and insulator cards to build a safe cable, and you win cards by saying which box a thing belongs in and why. Some cards belong in neither box, and those are the most useful.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile in the middle of a table with their fronts facing up, and two players sitting opposite each other.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put the pile front side up.

setup.art: One player holding the top card and speaking, while the other player lifts the card's edge to read the back.
setup.caption: 2. Say conductor, insulator or it depends, and give your reason. The other player reads the back.

setup.art: A row of four cards on the table with two more cards laid across the top of them like a cover.
setup.caption: 3. A safe cable: four conductors in a row, with two insulators laid over them.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a thing on the front, and its box with the reason on the back

items.f: The copper inside an electric cord
items.b: Conductor. Copper has free electrons, and very little holds them back.
Conductor. Steel is a metal, with electrons free to move through the whole spoon.
Conductor. The foil is aluminium, the same metal as the big power lines across the country.
Conductor. Coins are made of metal.

items.f: The lead of a pencil, touched at both ends
items.b: Conductor. The lead is graphite, a form of carbon with one free electron on each atom. It conducts less well than a metal.
Conductor. Sea water is full of ions from dissolved salt.
Conductor. Gold is one of the best. The tiny contacts inside a phone are coated with it.

items.f: The brass pins of a plug
items.b: Conductor. The pins must carry the current from the socket into the cord.
Conductor. Iron is a metal.

items.f: A tumbler of water with two spoons of salt stirred in
items.b: Conductor. The salt has broken into ions, which carry the current. A torch bulb may still stay dark, but an LED glows.

items.f: The plastic coat on a wire
items.b: Insulator. Every electron in the plastic is held in place. The coat keeps the current in the copper.

items.f: A line worker's thick rubber glove, dry and tested
items.b: Insulator. Rubber holds its electrons firmly. The glove is made and checked for this job.
Insulator. Dry wood has almost no free charges.

items.f: A glass marble at room temperature
items.b: Insulator. Cold glass holds its charges in place.
Insulator. Dry cotton has no free charges.

items.f: A ceramic disc on a power-line tower
items.b: Insulator. The discs hold the bare live wire away from the steel tower.

items.f: The plastic cover of a wall switch
items.b: Insulator. The cover stands between your finger and the live metal behind.
Insulator. Wax was one of the first insulators people found.
It depends on the push and on the minerals in the water. A 3 volt bulb tester stays dark. An LED glows faintly. At 230 volts, tap water carries a deadly current.
It depends on the push. Air insulates very well, until the push reaches about 30,000 volts across each centimetre. Then the air conducts, as a spark or as lightning.
It depends on water. A dead dry branch insulates. A living branch full of sap, or any wet branch, conducts.
It depends on the push and on wetness. At 3 volts, dry skin lets almost nothing through. Wet skin at 230 volts lets through enough to kill.

items.f: A kite string near a power line
items.b: It depends on what the string is made of and whether it is wet. Dry cotton insulates. Wet string or string coated with metal conducts. Never fly a kite near power lines.

items.f: A piece of silicon from a computer chip
items.b: It depends on what the engineers ask of it. Silicon is a semiconductor. A tiny push from a neighbouring part switches it between conducting and not conducting.

rules: The aim is to build a safe cable: four conductor cards in a row, with two insulator cards laid over them as the cover.
Shuffle the cards and put the pile on the table with the fronts up. Nobody looks at the backs.
On your turn, take the top card. Say 'conductor', 'insulator' or 'it depends', and give your reason. If you say 'it depends', say what it depends on.
The player on your left turns the card over and reads the back aloud. If your box was right, you keep the card. If not, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
Add a conductor card to your row and an insulator card to your cover. An 'it depends' card is wild. You may use it as a conductor or as an insulator.
If you win a card your cable does not need, give it to any player who needs it.
The first player to finish a safe cable wins. If the pile runs out first, the player with the most cards in a cable wins. Equal numbers share the win.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to finish a safe cable. Next time, try to do it in fewer.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and shuffle them. Put the pile front side up. Read the rules together and show what a finished safe cable looks like, using six blank scraps of paper.
flow.say: A cable needs both kinds. Four conductors carry the current. Two insulators keep it in. You win a card by naming its box and giving a reason.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Fronts up. A safe cable needs four conductors and two insulators.
flow.parent: Cards are printed two-sided. If you cannot print two-sided, write each back by hand, or keep the list of backs with one player as the checker.
flow.context: This is the first step of Safe Cable. You set up and learn the aim.

flow.do: Play the first two rounds slowly. After each card, the reader reads the whole back aloud. Talk about the reason, not only the box.
flow.say: Take the top card. Which box, and why? Now let us hear the back. Did your reason match?
flow.kid: Take a card. Say the box and your reason. Listen to the back.

ask.q: What do all the conductor cards so far have inside them?
good: Charges that are free to move.
Something that can carry the current.

flow.parent: A right box with a weak reason still wins the card. Ask for a better reason next time. If a child argues well that a card on the back is wrong, listen: some of these are worth arguing about.
flow.context: In this step, you play two slow rounds and talk about the reasons.

flow.do: Play on until someone finishes a safe cable or the pile runs out. Each time an 'it depends' card comes up, the player must say what it depends on before the back is read.
flow.say: Keep playing. An 'it depends' card can be either kind, so it is the most useful card. But first you must say what it depends on.
flow.kid: Keep playing. For 'it depends', say what it depends on. First safe cable wins.
flow.context: In this step, you play the game to the end.

flow.do: Lay all 24 cards out in one long line, from the best conductor to the best insulator. Move cards until everyone agrees, or agrees to disagree.
flow.say: The game used two boxes and a wild card. Now forget the boxes. Put every card in one line, from conducts best to conducts least. Where is it hard to choose?
flow.kid: Lay all the cards in one line. Best conductor to best insulator.
flow.parent: There is no exact right order for the 'it depends' cards, and that is the point. Ask where they would move if they got wet, or if the push were 230 volts.
flow.think: Why was the wild card the most useful card in the game?
flow.context: This is the last step of Safe Cable. You turn two boxes into one line.

experiments.title: The Water Test: which water lights the LED?
experiments.question: Does water let electricity through? Does it matter what is dissolved in the water, and does it matter which tester you ask?
experiments.predict: Before you build anything, look at the five cups. For each one, guess how brightly the LED will glow, from 0 to 3. Give a reason for each guess. Will sugar water and salt water be the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Only what is in the cup changes. Every cup has the same amount of water. The two wire ends are fixed one finger-width apart on a card, and dip to the same depth each time. The room stays equally dim. Rinse and wipe the wire ends before each new cup, so no salt is carried across. Test from the plainest water to the saltiest. Dip three times in each cup, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 2 fresh AA cells in a holder, or two cells taped end to end
3 wires with bare metal ends, or with clips and 2 steel paper clips to hold in them
red LEDs, the small 5 millimetre kind (one to use and one spare)
a 2.5 volt torch bulb in a holder, or the bulb from an old torch
5 small plastic cups or bowls of the same size, and a plastic mug of tap water for rinsing
drinking water, tap water, salt, sugar, half a lemon and a teaspoon
a strip of thick card as long as your hand, sticky tape and an old cloth
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Use only AA cells. Never test water with anything that is joined to a wall socket. Do not drink any water that the wires have been in, because a little metal dissolves into it. Pour it down the sink and wash the cups.
experiments.record: Write the three glow scores for each cup. Then draw a bar for each cup, as tall as its usual score. Under the bars, write one line: what I thought, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you dip a home-made tester into five kinds of water. You find out whether water conducts, and what in the water does the carrying.

setup.art: A cell holder with two AA cells, a red LED with one long leg and one short leg, and three wires. One wire runs from the plus end of the holder to the long leg, one from the short leg to a free end, one from the minus end to a free end.
setup.caption: 1. Build the tester. The long leg of the LED goes towards the plus end.

setup.art: A strip of card with the two free wire ends taped to it one finger-width apart, about two finger-widths of bare metal hanging below the edge of the card.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the two free ends to a card, one finger-width apart.

setup.art: Five identical small plastic cups in a row labelled A to E, each half full, with a teaspoon, a bowl of salt, a bowl of sugar and half a lemon beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Five cups: drinking water, tap water, sugar water, lemon water, salt water.

setup.art: A hand resting the card across the rim of a cup so both wire ends hang in the water, the red LED glowing faintly, and a second hand cupped round the LED to shade it.
setup.caption: 4. Rest the card on the cup. Count to five. Score the glow from 0 to 3.

flow.do: Set out the five empty cups and the water, salt, sugar and lemon. Say what will go in each cup. Ask for a guess for each cup, from 0 for no glow to 3 for bright. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will ask five kinds of water one question. Will you let electricity through? Guess a score for each cup. Tell me your reason for each one.
flow.kid: Guess first. How bright will the LED be in each cup? Say why.

ask.q: Will sugar water and salt water score the same? Why?
good: No, salt is different from sugar.
I think water alone is enough.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Many children, and many adults, expect all water to conduct equally. With 2 to 4 children, each writes a guess before anyone speaks.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Test. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Join one wire from the plus end of the cell holder to the long leg of the LED. Join a second wire to the short leg. Join a third wire to the minus end. Tape the two free ends to the card, one finger-width apart. Leave two finger-widths of bare metal below the card.
flow.say: Now we build the tester. The long leg of the LED goes towards the plus end. To check it, touch the two free ends together for one second only. Does the LED light?
flow.kid: Build the tester. Long leg to plus. Touch the two ends together for one second. Does the LED light?
flow.parent: If the LED stays dark, turn the LED round, because an LED works one way only. Press every joint firmly. Do not hold the two ends together for longer than a second: with nothing in the gap, too much current flows and the LED can burn out. That is why there is a spare. If the wire ends have less than two finger-widths of bare metal, clip or twist each one onto a straightened steel paper clip. The metal is bare, not pointed, but mind eyes with younger children.
flow.context: In this step, you build the LED tester and check that it works.

flow.do: Label the cups A to E. Pour half a small tumbler of drinking water into A, C, D and E. Pour the same amount of tap water into B. Stir one level teaspoon of sugar into C. Squeeze one teaspoon of lemon juice into D. Stir one level teaspoon of salt into E.
flow.say: Every cup gets the same amount of water. A is plain drinking water. B is tap water. C gets sugar, D gets lemon and E gets salt. Stir until you cannot see the sugar or the salt.
flow.kid: Fill five cups the same. A is plain. B is tap water. C sugar, D lemon, E salt.
flow.parent: Half a small tumbler is about 100 millilitres. Filtered or bottled drinking water is best for A, C, D and E, because it holds fewer minerals than tap water. If you have only tap water, use it for all five and leave cup B out. Rinse the spoon between cups.
flow.context: In this step, you make five cups of water that differ in one way only.

flow.do: Dim the room. Rest the card on cup A so both wire ends are in the water. Count to five and score the glow. Lift, and dip twice more. Rinse the ends in the mug and wipe them. Do the same for B, C, D and E, in that order.
flow.say: Dip, count to five and look closely. Cup your hand round the LED. Zero is no glow, one is faint, two is clear, three is bright. Rinse and wipe before the next cup.
flow.kid: Dip in cup A. Count to five. Score the glow. Rinse and wipe. Now B, C, D and E.
flow.parent: Typical results: A gives no glow or the faintest glow. B is faint. C is the same as A. D is clear. E is bright. Tap water differs from city to city: hard borewell water glows more than soft river water. If even cup E gives nothing, turn the LED round, press the joints, and move the wire ends closer without letting them touch. If it still fails, tape a third cell into the row and test all five cups again with three cells. Small bubbles on a wire are normal.

check.q: Sugar water scored the same as plain water. Salt water scored much higher. What does that tell you?
options: Anything dissolved in water helps it conduct
Dissolving is not enough. The salt adds something sugar does not
check.why: Both dissolve fully, so dissolving alone cannot be the reason. Salt breaks into charged pieces called ions, and sugar stays as whole pieces with no charge. If you chose the second answer, look at cup C again: sugar is dissolved in it, and the glow did not grow.

flow.context: In this step, you test the five cups and score the glow.

flow.do: Go back to cup A. Add one pinch of salt, stir ten times, dip and score. Add a second, third and fourth pinch, scoring after each one.
flow.say: Now change cup A a little at a time. One pinch of salt, stir, dip and score. Then another. What happens to the glow with each pinch?
flow.kid: Add one pinch of salt to cup A. Stir. Dip and score. Do it four times.

good: It goes up in steps, with no sudden jump.

flow.parent: The glow grows step by step. There is no pinch at which the water suddenly turns from an insulator into a conductor. Let your child notice this and say it in their own words.
flow.context: In this step, you add salt a pinch at a time and watch the glow grow.

flow.do: Take the LED out of the tester and put the torch bulb in its place. Dip the ends into cup E, the saltiest. Look at the bulb. Then touch the two ends together to check that the bulb works.
flow.say: Guess first. The LED was bright in cup E. Will the torch bulb light too? Now try it. Then touch the ends together.
flow.kid: Swap the LED for the torch bulb. Dip in cup E. Does the bulb light?

ask.q: The LED says yes and the bulb says no. Is salt water a conductor?

flow.parent: The bulb stays dark in salt water and lights when the ends touch. A torch bulb needs about a hundred times more current than an LED before it glows. Do not settle the question for your child. This disagreement is the heart of the lesson.
flow.context: In this step, you ask the same salt water the same question with a different tester.

flow.do: Ask your child to write three lines: what I thought, what I saw, and why. Then take the cells out of the holder. Pour every cup down the sink and wash the cups.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Then we pour the water away, because nobody should drink it.
flow.kid: Write what you thought, what you saw, and why. Pour the water away. Do not drink it.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that plain water let very little through, that salt and lemon added something that carries current, and that sugar did not. After your child has said this, give the word ions. Then say what this test cannot tell us: it cannot show the ions themselves, and it cannot say that cup A lets nothing through. A more sensitive tester might still find a tiny current.
flow.think: If a better tester found a tiny current even in the purest water, would any water be an insulator?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Water Test. You explain your results and clear up.

experiments.title: Two Testers: when the bulb says no, does the LED agree?
experiments.question: Do a bulb tester and an LED tester sort the same ten things into the same boxes?
experiments.predict: Put the ten things into three piles before you test. Pile one: it will light the bulb. Pile two: it will light only the LED. Pile three: it will light neither. Give a reason for where you put the pencil, the tomato and your fingertip.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two cells and the same wires for every thing. Press the two wire ends on firmly, one finger-width apart, each time. Test in the same dim room. Test each thing twice. Always use the bulb first. Use the LED only on things that left the bulb dark, because a good conductor lets through enough current to burn out an LED.

materials.item: the tester from the Water Test: 2 AA cells in a holder and 3 wires
a 2.5 volt torch bulb in a holder
a red LED
a steel spoon, a coin, a strip of kitchen foil, a plastic ruler and an eraser
a pencil with the lead showing at both ends (sharpen both ends with a pencil sharpener)
a dry ice-cream stick or wooden spoon, and a thick slice of raw tomato or potato
a strip of newspaper, and a spoonful of salt water in a saucer
the results table and a pencil

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw one long line across a page. Write 'conducts best' at one end and 'conducts least' at the other. Place all ten things along the line where you think they belong.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you test ten things with a torch bulb and then with an LED. You find out whether two honest testers can give two different answers about the same thing.

setup.art: Ten things laid in a row on a table: a steel spoon, a coin, a strip of foil, a pencil with lead showing at both ends, a plastic ruler, an eraser, an ice-cream stick, a slice of tomato, a strip of newspaper, and a child's hand.
setup.caption: 1. Ten things to test. Sort them into three piles by guessing.

setup.art: The two free wire ends of a bulb tester pressed onto the two ends of a pencil lead, the torch bulb glowing a dim orange.
setup.caption: 2. The bulb goes first. Bright, dim or dark?

setup.art: The same tester with a red LED in place of the bulb, the wire ends pushed into a slice of tomato one finger-width apart, the LED glowing.
setup.caption: 3. If the bulb stayed dark, ask again with the LED.

flow.do: Lay out the ten things: spoon, coin, foil, pencil, ruler, eraser, dry stick, tomato slice, dry newspaper strip and a fingertip. Ask your child to sort them into three piles by guessing. Write the pile number for each in the table.
flow.say: Pile one will light the bulb. Pile two will light only the LED, which needs far less current. Pile three will light neither. Where does each thing go? Tell me why.
flow.kid: Sort ten things into three piles. Bulb, only LED, or neither. Say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the piles. The pencil, the tomato and the fingertip are the interesting ones. A fingertip cannot go in a pile, so write its number in the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Testers. You sort by guessing before you test.

flow.do: Put the torch bulb in the tester. Press the two wire ends onto each thing in turn, one finger-width apart. For the pencil, press one end on each tip of the lead. For the tomato, push both ends into the slice. Write bright, dim or dark.
flow.say: The bulb goes first, every time. Press both ends on firmly. Is the bulb bright, dim or dark? Test each thing twice.
flow.kid: Test each thing with the bulb. Press both wire ends on. Bright, dim or dark?

ask.q: Is the pencil like the spoon, like the ruler, or like neither?
good: Neither. It is dimmer than the spoon.

flow.parent: Typical results: spoon, coin and foil are bright. A whole pencil is dim or dark, and a short pencil stub is brighter. Everything else is dark. A 3 volt tester on a fingertip is harmless and gives no sensation. If the spoon gives nothing, the bulb is loose or a joint is not touching.
flow.context: In this step, you test all ten things with the torch bulb.

flow.do: Put the LED in place of the bulb, long leg towards plus. Test only the things that left the bulb dark. Never test the spoon, coin or foil with the LED. Write bright, faint or dark.
flow.say: Now ask again with the LED, but only where the bulb was dark. The spoon, coin and foil would burn the LED out. Dim the room and look closely.
flow.kid: Swap in the LED. Test only the things that left the bulb dark.
flow.parent: Typical results: the pencil is bright. The tomato or potato is faint to clear. Ruler, eraser, dry stick and dry paper are dark. A dry fingertip is usually dark, though a laboratory meter would find a tiny current through it. A dark LED does not prove that nothing at all gets through.

check.q: The bulb stayed dark on the tomato slice. The LED glowed. What is the best conclusion?
options: The tomato lets a small current through
check.why: The LED needs far less current than the bulb. A glow in the LED shows that some current passed, too little for the bulb. If you chose the insulator, remember that a dark bulb only tells you the current was below what a bulb needs. The bulb lit on the spoon, so it is not broken.

flow.context: In this step, you ask the same things again with a more sensitive tester.

flow.do: Test the dry newspaper strip with the LED. Then dip the strip in the saucer of salt water and test it again. Lick a fingertip, press both wire ends on it close together, and look once more.
flow.say: The paper was dark when dry. Guess what the LED will do when the same paper is wet with salt water. Now try it.
flow.kid: Test dry paper. Wet it with salt water. Test again. What changed?
flow.parent: The wet strip usually gives a faint to clear glow. The paper is the same paper. Only the water and the ions in it are new. A licked fingertip may give the faintest glow, or none.
flow.context: In this step, you change one thing about the paper and test it again.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask them to place all ten things along one line, from conducts best to conducts least.
flow.say: You made three piles at the start. Would you still use three piles? Put the ten things in one line, from the best conductor to the worst.
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Put the ten things in one line.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the two testers disagreed on some things, and that the things fall along a line, not into two boxes. After your child has said this, explain that a bulb needs a large current and an LED a small one. Then say what the test cannot show: where the ruler and the eraser sit on the line, because neither tester is sensitive enough.
flow.think: If you had a tester a million times more sensitive than the LED, which pile would shrink?
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Testers. You explain your results.

activities.title: Coin Train: charges that are free and charges that are held

materials.item: 11 coins of the same size
2 rulers or 2 books to make a straight track
sticky tape

activities.record: Draw the two coin trains. Under each, write which material it stands for and one way the model is not like the real thing.
activities.context: In this activity, you push a line of coins that are free to slide, and then a line of coins that are taped down. It is a model of why a metal conducts and plastic does not.

setup.art: Ten coins touching in a straight line between two rulers on a table, with a finger about to push an eleventh coin into one end.
setup.caption: 1. Ten free coins in a track. Push one more in at one end.

setup.art: The same ten coins each held down with a strip of sticky tape, and a finger pushing at the end coin, which does not move.
setup.caption: 2. Tape every coin down. Push again.

flow.do: Lay two rulers side by side, a coin's width apart. Put ten coins in the track, touching. Ask what will happen at the far end if one more coin is pushed in. Then push it in slowly.
flow.say: Watch the far end. I push one coin in here. What happens there, and how soon? How far did each coin move?
flow.kid: Line up ten coins. Push one more in. Watch the far end.

ask.q: Did the coin you pushed travel to the far end?
good: No. It only moved one place.
They all moved a little, together.

flow.parent: A coin leaves the far end at once, yet each coin moved only one coin-width. A metal wire is like this: full of free electrons that all shift together.
flow.context: This is the first step of Coin Train. The free coins stand for the free electrons in a metal.

flow.do: Tape each of the ten coins to the table. Push the eleventh coin against the end of the line with the same gentle push.
flow.say: Now every coin is held in its place. Push with the same gentle push. What happens at the far end?
flow.kid: Tape every coin down. Push again. What happens now?
flow.parent: Nothing moves. Plastic and rubber are like this: every electron is held by its own atom. A much harder push would tear the tape. That is like a spark breaking through an insulator.
flow.context: In this step, the taped coins stand for the held electrons in an insulator.

flow.do: Ask which train stands for copper and which for plastic. Then ask how the model is not like the real thing.
flow.say: Which train is the copper wire? Which is the plastic coat? Every model is wrong somewhere. Where is this one wrong?
flow.kid: Which train is copper? Which is plastic? Where is the model wrong?
flow.parent: Good answers: real electrons push each other without touching. A wire is a loop, so nothing falls off the end. In salt water two kinds of charge move in opposite directions.
flow.think: How would you change the coin train to show salt water, where two kinds of ions move opposite ways?
flow.context: This is the last step of Coin Train. You say what the model shows and where it fails.

activities.title: Plug Detectives: find the conductors and the insulators

materials.item: a three-pin plug on an appliance that a grown-up has switched off and unplugged
a torch that opens
paper, a pencil, and an orange and a blue crayon

activities.safety: A grown-up switches off and pulls out the plug before anyone looks at it. Nobody touches a socket. Nobody opens a plug or an appliance that runs from the wall.
activities.record: Keep the two drawings: the plug and the torch, with conductors in orange and insulators in blue.
activities.context: In this activity, you look closely at a plug and a torch and colour in which parts are conductors and which are insulators. You find out why each part is made of what it is made of.

setup.art: A three-pin plug lying on a table well away from the wall, with its cord, and a child drawing it large on paper.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up unplugs it. Look, and draw it large.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a plug with the three pins coloured orange and the body and cord coloured blue.
setup.caption: 2. Orange for conductors. Blue for insulators.

setup.art: An opened torch with its parts laid in a row: two cells, a spring, a metal strip, a switch, a small bulb and the plastic case, with a finger tracing the path.
setup.caption: 3. Open a torch and trace the path with a finger.

flow.do: A grown-up switches off one appliance, pulls the plug out and lays the plug on a table. Look at the pins, the body and the cord. Count the pins. Find the pin that is thicker and longer than the others.
flow.say: I have unplugged it, so it is safe to look at. What is each part made of? Which parts would you be willing to hold, if it were plugged in?
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up to unplug it. Look at the pins, the body and the cord.

ask.q: Why are the pins metal and the body plastic?
good: The pins must carry current in.
The body is where fingers go.
Plastic keeps the current away from my hand.

flow.parent: The pins are brass. The body is hard plastic. The thick top pin is the earth pin. Some chargers have two pins and a body made fully of plastic. They need no earth pin, because no metal part can be touched.
flow.context: This is the first step of Plug Detectives. You look at a plug that is safely out of the wall.

flow.do: Draw the plug and its cord large on paper. Colour every conductor orange and every insulator blue. Then draw what you think is inside the cord.
flow.say: Colour the parts that carry current orange. Colour the parts that hold it back blue. What do you think is hidden inside the cord? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Draw the plug. Orange for conductors. Blue for insulators. Guess what is inside the cord.
flow.parent: Inside the cord are three copper wires. Each has its own plastic coat, and one more coat goes round all three. The coats keep the three wires from touching each other.

check.q: The earth pin is longer than the other two pins. What is the best reason?
options: It carries the most current every day
It joins first and leaves last, so the body is earthed whenever the others are live
It makes the plug easier to hold
check.why: A longer pin touches its socket hole first when the plug goes in and leaves last when it comes out. So the metal body is always joined to the ground while current can flow. On a normal day the earth wire carries no current at all. If you chose the first answer, remember it works only when there is a fault.

flow.context: In this step, you draw a plug as a map of conductors and insulators.

flow.do: Open the torch and lay out the parts. With a finger, trace the path from one end of the cells, through the bulb, and back. Find the place where the switch makes a gap. Draw the torch and colour it orange and blue.
flow.say: Trace the whole loop with your finger. Where does the path go through metal? Where does an insulator stop it? What does the switch do to the path?
flow.kid: Open the torch. Trace the loop with a finger. Find the gap the switch makes.
flow.parent: In many torches the path runs through a spring, a metal strip along the case, the switch and the bulb. If your torch has a metal case, the case itself may be part of the loop. A torch is safe to open because it runs on cells.
flow.think: A switch is a small insulating gap that you can close. What is the insulator inside the gap of most switches?
flow.context: This is the last step of Plug Detectives. You read a torch as a loop of conductors with insulators around it.

activities.title: Safety Walk with a Why: the insulators that guard our home

materials.item: paper on a hard board, and a pencil
a large sheet of paper and crayons for a poster

activities.safety: A grown-up walks with the child. Look only. Nobody touches a socket, a bare wire or the meter board.
activities.record: Keep the list of what you found, and put the poster of five rules, each with its because, near the kitchen.
activities.context: In this activity, you walk through your home and find each place where an insulator stands between a person and 230 volts. You write each safety rule with the reason for it.

setup.art: A child with a clipboard and a grown-up standing in a room, the child pointing at a switch plate on the wall from an arm's length away.
setup.caption: 1. Walk and look. Where does an insulator guard you?

setup.art: A close view of trouble spots: a cracked plug, a cord with its coat worn through, and an extension board beside a wet sink, each circled in red.
setup.caption: 2. Look for insulators that are broken, worn or wet.

setup.art: A hand-made poster with five short rules, each followed by the word 'because' and a reason, with small drawings.
setup.caption: 3. Write five rules. Each rule has a because.

flow.do: Walk through each room together. Find six places where an insulator covers a conductor: a switch plate, a plug body, a cord, an appliance handle, a bulb holder, the cover of the meter board. Look from an arm's length away and write each one down.
flow.say: Behind this plastic is metal at 230 volts. What is the insulator here? What would happen if it were not there?
flow.kid: Walk with a grown-up. Find six insulators that cover a conductor. Look only.

ask.q: Which appliances have a metal body, and what kind of plug do they have?
good: The fridge, the mixer, the iron.
The third pin is for the earth wire.

flow.parent: Metal-bodied appliances such as a fridge, an iron, a mixer and a wet grinder should all have three-pin plugs. At the meter board, show the small switches from a distance and say that they cut the current when there is a fault.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Safety Walk. You find the insulators that are doing their job.

flow.do: Walk again and look for trouble. Look for a cracked plug, a worn cord and a joint wrapped in tape. Look for a loose socket, a board near water, and a two-pin plug on a metal appliance. Write each one down. The grown-up decides what to mend and when to call an electrician.
flow.say: Now look for insulators that are broken, worn or wet. Do not touch. Tell me, and I will write it down. Which one should we mend first?
flow.kid: Look for broken, worn or wet insulators. Do not touch. Tell a grown-up.
flow.parent: Children are often better at spotting these than adults who have stopped seeing them. Take each find seriously. A home with none is also a good result.
flow.context: In this step, you look for places where an insulator has failed.

flow.do: Write five safety rules for your home on the large sheet. After each rule write 'because' and the reason. Draw a small picture for each.
flow.say: A rule with no reason is easy to forget. Write five rules, and give each one its because. Use what you know about conductors and insulators.
flow.kid: Write five rules. Each needs a because. Draw a picture for each.
flow.parent: Rules to choose from: dry hands before any switch. Hold the plug, not the cord. Nothing metal goes into a socket or a toaster. Keep kites and long poles away from overhead lines. Stay away from fallen wires and flooded poles. Tell a grown-up about any tingle. If someone is getting a shock, do not touch them: switch off at the main switch.
flow.think: Which of your rules is about a conductor, and which is about an insulator that might fail?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Safety Walk. You turn what you found into rules with reasons.

projects.title: The Secret-Wire Quiz Board

materials.item: a piece of stiff card about the size of a notebook page
kitchen foil, and wide sticky tape
10 steel paper clips
the bulb tester: 2 AA cells in a holder, a torch bulb in a holder and 3 wires
a spare 2.5 volt torch bulb
paper, a pen and scissors

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Use only AA cells.
projects.record: Keep the board. Change the questions each week by taping on a new sheet. On the back, write which parts are conductors and which are insulators.
projects.context: In this project, you build a quiz board with hidden foil paths on the back. The bulb lights only when a question is matched to its right answer. You use conductors and insulators on purpose, as an appliance maker does.

setup.art: The front of a card with five questions written down the left side and five answers down the right side in a different order, with a paper clip on the edge beside each one.
setup.caption: 1. Five questions on the left, five answers on the right, a paper clip beside each.

setup.art: The back of the card: five folded foil strips, each running from a left clip to a right clip, crossing over one another, each fully covered with sticky tape.
setup.caption: 2. On the back, a foil strip joins each question to its answer. Tape covers every strip.

setup.art: A child touching one tester wire to a question's clip and the other to an answer's clip, with the torch bulb glowing.
setup.caption: 3. Touch a question and an answer. The bulb lights only for the right pair.

flow.do: Write five questions about this lesson down the left side of the card. Write the five answers down the right side, in a mixed-up order. Slide a paper clip over the edge beside each question and each answer.
flow.say: Write five questions that you can now answer. Mix up the answers on the other side. Each one gets a paper clip on the edge.
flow.kid: Write five questions on the left. Mix up five answers on the right. Clip each one.
flow.parent: A question may be as simple as 'What carries current in salt water?' with the answer 'ions'. The clips must grip the card so that part of each clip is on the back.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Quiz Board. You make the front.

flow.do: A grown-up helps cut five foil strips, each two fingers wide. Fold each strip in three along its length. On the back of the card, lay one strip from a question's clip to its answer's clip, tucked under both clips. Cover the whole strip with tape. Then lay the next strip.
flow.say: Each foil strip is a wire. It must touch both clips. Cover each strip fully with tape before you lay the next one across it. Why do you think the tape matters?
flow.kid: Fetch a grown-up. Join each question to its answer with foil. Cover each strip with tape.

ask.q: What would happen if two foil strips touched where they cross?
good: The bulb would light for a wrong answer.
The current could go down the wrong strip.

flow.parent: The tape is the insulator, like the plastic coat on each wire in a cord. Press the foil flat under each clip. Folded foil is stronger and tears less.
flow.context: In this step, you make five hidden conductors and insulate each one from the others.

flow.do: Touch one free end of the bulb tester to a question's clip and the other to an answer's clip. Try every answer for the first question. The bulb should light for one pair only. Mend any fault.
flow.say: Test each question against all five answers. For how many answers does the bulb light? If it lights for a wrong one, where could the fault be?
flow.kid: Touch a question clip and an answer clip. The bulb lights for one pair only.
flow.parent: If the bulb lights for a wrong pair, two strips are touching: add tape between them. If it never lights for the right pair, the foil is not under a clip, or the foil has torn.
flow.context: In this step, you test the board and find faults.

flow.do: Give the board and the tester to someone who has not seen the back. Let them play. Ask them to guess how it works before you show them.
flow.say: Do not show the back yet. Let them play, and ask how they think it works. Then turn it over and explain it yourself.
flow.kid: Let someone play. Ask how they think it works. Then show the back.
