flow.context: In this step, someone else plays your board, and you explain it.

flow.do: On the back, label the conductors and the insulators. Then tape a new sheet of questions over the front, keeping the same clips.
flow.say: Name every conductor on your board, and every insulator. Which insulator did you add on purpose? Which ones were already there?
flow.kid: Label the conductors and the insulators. Then write five new questions.
flow.parent: Conductors: foil, clips, the tester's wires. Insulators: tape, card, and the air between the clips. Children often forget the card and the air.
flow.think: The air between the clips is an insulator you did not have to add. What would change if the board were dipped in salt water?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Quiz Board. You name each part by the job it does.

challenges.title: The Full Bucket Signal
challenges.problem: A bucket under a slow tap overflows when nobody is watching. Make a signal that lights when the water reaches a line you choose, three finger-widths below the rim.
constraints: Use only 2 or 3 AA cells. Nothing may be joined to a wall socket.
It must work with plain tap water. You may not add salt.
The light must go off again when the water goes down.
The cells and the LED must stay dry.
materials: the LED tester from the Water Test
a torch bulb in a holder
kitchen foil, card and sticky tape
a plastic mug or small bucket, and tap water
a piece of dry sponge or a plastic bottle cap
general: Tape the two wire ends inside the mug at the line, a finger-width apart. The rising water joins them.
Use two strips of foil in place of the bare wire ends, so more metal is in the water.
Hang the wire ends from a peg on the rim, so the height is easy to change.
creative: Two squares of foil as big as a matchbox, facing each other with a thin piece of dry sponge between. A large area and a small gap let far more current through tap water.

A floating bottle cap carrying a foil bridge. As the water rises, the bridge lifts and touches two foil pads above. The water never has to conduct. Use the torch bulb for this one, because foil touching foil would burn out an LED.
A third cell in the row, for a harder push.
challenges.your_turn: Design a signal for a real place in your home: the overhead tank, a plant saucer, the tray under the fridge. Draw it. Say what the conductors and insulators are. There is more than one good answer. What would rainwater, which holds very few ions, do to your design?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make water close a circuit, and then you make the signal brighter without adding salt. Real tank alarms work this way.

setup.art: A plastic mug with a line drawn inside, two wire ends hanging from a clothes peg on the rim down to the line, and the LED and cell holder on the table outside the mug.
setup.caption: 1. The wire ends hang at the line. The cells and LED stay outside.

setup.art: Water being poured slowly into the mug from a tumbler, reaching the wire ends, and the red LED beginning to glow faintly.
setup.caption: 2. Pour slowly. Does the LED light when the water reaches the line?

setup.art: Two squares of foil facing each other with a thin sponge between them, held by a peg, with a wire taped to each square.
setup.caption: 3. One way to make it brighter: bigger foil, closer together.

flow.do: Read the problem and the four rules together. Mark a line inside the mug. Ask your child to sketch a first idea, and to say where the conductors and insulators are.
flow.say: The water has to switch the light on by itself. What could the water join together? Sketch your first idea.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Mark a line in the mug. Sketch your first idea.
flow.parent: Do not give the design. Most children think of two wire ends at the line. That is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Full Bucket Signal. You read the problem and sketch.

flow.do: Build the first idea. Keep the cells and the LED outside the mug. Pour tap water in slowly with a tumbler and watch the LED as the water reaches the line. Then pour some out and watch again.
flow.say: Pour slowly. Tell me the moment the light comes on. How bright is it? Would you see it from across the room?
flow.kid: Build it. Pour water in slowly. Does the LED light at the line?

good: Tap water lets only a little through.

flow.parent: With thin wire ends in tap water, expect a faint glow that shows only in a dim room. That is the honest first result. It sets up the real problem, which is to make it brighter.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test your first design.

flow.do: Change one thing to make the glow brighter, and test again. Try more metal in the water, or a smaller gap, or a third cell. Write down which change helped most.
flow.say: You may not add salt. What else could let more current through the same water? Change one thing at a time, so you know what helped.
flow.kid: Make it brighter. No salt. Change one thing at a time.
flow.parent: Larger foil squares held close together help the most. The two squares must not touch. A dry sponge or a strip of plastic keeps them apart and lets water in between.

check.q: Two large foil squares close together glow brighter than two thin wire ends far apart. Why?
options: Foil is a better metal than wire
More water lies side by side between them, and the ions have less far to go
check.why: The water is the hard part of the path. A wide, short path of water lets more ions across each second than a narrow, long one. The metal hardly matters, because both foil and wire conduct far better than the water. If you chose the first answer, test a foil strip the same size as the wire end and see.

flow.context: In this step, you improve the design without changing the water.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a signal for a real place at home, and to label its conductors and insulators. Dry the wire ends and take the cells out of the holder.
flow.say: Where at home would a signal like this be useful? Draw one for that place. Which parts are conductors, and which are insulators?
flow.kid: Draw a signal for a real place at home. Label conductors and insulators.
flow.parent: Many overhead tank alarms sold in India work exactly like this, with two metal points at the full line. There is no single best design. Ask what would go wrong with each idea.
flow.think: Your signal uses water as a switch. What else in your home is a switch that you never thought of as one?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Full Bucket Signal. You design one of your own.

quiz.p: Riya, a girl in your class, tests five cups of water. She does not rinse the wires between cups. What goes wrong?
opts: The wires stop working
Salt is carried into the next cup
Nothing goes wrong
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing only. Salt left on the wires changes the next cup too, so its score is too high. If you chose 'nothing', think about what the wet wire ends are carrying.

quiz.p: Which tester can show the smallest current?
opts: A tester with a red LED
A tester with a torch bulb
Both show exactly the same
quiz.why: An LED glows with about a hundredth of the current a torch bulb needs. So it catches currents the bulb misses.

quiz.p: What is inside a copper wire before it is joined to a cell?
opts: Nothing. The cell fills it up
Tiny sparks waiting to jump
Free electrons, all along the wire
quiz.why: The wire is already full of free electrons. The cell only pushes them. If you chose the first answer, think of the coin train: the coins were there before the push.

opts: Rubber has no electrons in it
Its electrons are held firmly by their atoms
Rubber is soft and bends
quiz.why: Every material has electrons. In rubber none are free to move, so a push moves almost no charge. Softness has nothing to do with it: hard glass insulates too.

quiz.p: You add salt to plain water one pinch at a time. What does the LED do?
opts: It jumps from dark to full at one pinch
It does not change
It grows brighter with each pinch
quiz.why: Each pinch adds more ions, and more ions carry more current. There is no pinch where water suddenly becomes a conductor.

opts: Rainwater caught in a clean plastic bowl
Sea water
Filtered drinking water
quiz.why: Sea water holds the most ions by far. Rainwater holds the fewest of the three. The more ions, the better water conducts.

quiz.p: Why is 230 volts dangerous when 1.5 volts is not?
opts: The harder push drives a large current through a body
Mains is a different kind of electricity
A cell has no electricity in it
quiz.why: It is the same electricity. 230 volts pushes more than 150 times as hard, so far more current gets through skin. A large current through the chest can stop the heart.

quiz.p: Dry skin is a perfect insulator.
quiz.why: False. Dry skin holds back much more than wet skin does, but never everything. At 230 volts enough current passes through dry skin to do harm.

quiz.p: Why are the handles of an electrician's pliers covered in rubber?
opts: To make the pliers heavier
Only to give a better grip
So current cannot pass from the metal to the hand
quiz.why: The metal jaws may touch a live wire. The rubber is an insulator between the metal and the hand. A grip helps too, but it is not the main reason.

quiz.p: What does the earth wire join the metal body of a fridge to?
opts: The ground
The switch
The bulb inside the fridge
quiz.why: The earth wire runs from the metal body to the ground. If a loose wire makes the body live, the current takes this easy path, and a safety switch cuts the supply.

quiz.p: Which sentence about conductors and insulators is the most accurate?
opts: Every material is fully one or fully the other
Only metals have charges inside them
They are two ends of one long scale
quiz.why: Materials range from silver to rubber, with pencil lead, salt water, silicon and skin in between. All materials have charges inside. What differs is how free the charges are.

quiz.p: A mixer gives your hand a tingle. What is the right thing to do?
opts: Touch it again to make sure
Switch off at the main switch and tell a grown-up
Wipe it with a wet cloth and carry on
quiz.why: A tingle means current is reaching the metal body, so an insulator has failed. Cut the supply first, then get an electrician. Touching again, or adding water, gives the current a better path through you.

quiz.p: Someone is getting a shock from an appliance. What should you do first?
opts: Switch off at the main switch without touching them
Pull them away with your hands
Throw water on the appliance
quiz.why: A body conducts, so touching the person can pass the current through you too. Cutting the supply ends the danger for everyone. Water would make every path easier.

quiz.p: Which of these is still an open question for scientists?
opts: Whether copper conducts
How ceramic superconductors work
Whether salt dissolves in water
quiz.why: Ceramic superconductors were found in 1986, and physicists still argue about what pairs up the electrons inside them. The other two were settled long ago.

items.p: A tester's bulb lights when a key is put across the gap. What does that show?
opts: The key makes electricity
The key lets current through
The key is a magnet
items.why: The bulb lights only when the loop is complete, so the key must have carried the current across the gap. The cells make the push, not the key.

items.p: Which part of an electric wire is the insulator?
opts: The plastic coat
The copper strands
The bare end
items.why: The plastic coat holds its charges still, so current stays in the copper. The bare end is copper too, left uncovered so it can be joined.

items.p: A plastic ruler has no electric charges inside it.
items.why: False. Every material is made of atoms full of charges. In plastic the charges are held in place. That is what makes plastic an insulator.

items.p: Sugar water conducts much better than plain water.
items.why: False. Sugar dissolves, but it stays as whole molecules with no charge. With no new ions, the water conducts as it did before.

items.p: The charged atoms that carry current through salt water are called ____.
items.why: Salt breaks into sodium ions and chloride ions in water. They drift to the two wires and carry the current.

items.p: In a metal, the tiny charged particles that are free to move are called ____.
items.why: Each metal atom lets go of one or more electrons. These belong to the whole piece and drift when a cell pushes them.

items.p: Sort these by what a 3 volt bulb tester would show.
items.why: The spoon, the foil and the coin are metals with free electrons. The eraser, the marble and the dry wood hold their charges too firmly for a 3 volt push.

items.p: Match each part to its job.
pairs: the brass pins of a plug
the plastic body of a plug
keeps fingers away from live metal
leads a fault current to the ground
opens and closes a gap in the loop
items.why: Conductors lead the current where it is wanted. Insulators keep it away from everywhere else. A switch is a conductor that can be moved to close an insulating gap.

items.p: Put these in order, from conducts best to conducts least.
items.why: Copper has the most free charges. Salt water has many ions, tap water has few, and dry plastic has almost no free charge at all.

items.p: Why must hands be dry before touching a switch?
opts: Wet hands are slippery
Water makes switches rust at once
Wet skin lets far more current through
items.why: Dry skin holds back most of a current. Wet skin is about 100 times easier to pass, and the water can also creep into the switch to the live metal.

items.p: Explain why an electric wire is made of two materials, not one.
items.a: The copper inside is a conductor, so it carries the current where it is needed. The plastic outside is an insulator, so the current cannot leave the copper to reach a hand or another wire.
items.why: A strong answer names both jobs: leading the current, and keeping it in. It may add that two bare wires touching would make a short path.

items.p: Draw a cup of salt water with two wires in it. Show what moves, and which way.
items.a: Two wires in a cup. Small balls marked plus drift towards one wire and balls marked minus drift towards the other.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two kinds of ions moving in opposite directions. It shows no electrons swimming alone through the water.

items.p: Here is a three-pin plug with its cord. Label each part.
labels: one of the two current pins
a: the thick, long top pin: earth pin
either lower pin: one of the two current pins
the part you hold: plastic body
items.why: The top pin is thicker and longer, so it joins first. The two lower pins carry the current in and out. The body and the cord's coat are insulators.
items.art: A three-pin plug seen from the pin side with a length of cord, with four blank label boxes joined by lines to the top pin, a lower pin, the body and the cord.

items.p: An LED glows in a cup of water where a torch bulb stays dark. Why?
opts: The LED makes its own electricity
The LED needs far less current to glow
Torch bulbs never work in water
items.why: The same small current flows in both tests. It is enough for an LED and far too little for a bulb's thin wire to get hot.

items.p: Write one safety rule for your home. Then write the reason for it.
items.a: Any true rule with a correct reason. For example: I dry my hands before touching a switch, because wet skin lets about 100 times more current through.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason that uses conductors, insulators, ions or the size of the push. A rule with no reason is only half an answer.

items.p: Salt and sugar both dissolve. Why does only salt make water conduct well?
opts: Salt is heavier than sugar
Salt breaks into charged ions
Sugar blocks the wires
items.why: Salt splits into ions with plus and minus charges, which can carry current. Sugar molecules stay whole and have no charge to carry.

items.p: A bird stands with both feet on one bare power line and is unharmed. Why?
opts: Birds are too small to conduct
Her feet are made of rubber
Nothing pushes current through her body
items.why: Both feet are on the same wire, so there is no push from one foot to the other. If she touched a second wire or the tower, current would pass through her.

items.p: A 1.5 volt cell is safe to hold because skin can hold back so gentle a push.
items.why: True. Skin has a large resistance, and 1.5 volts sends almost no current through it. The same skin does not hold back 230 volts.

items.p: On a normal day, the earth wire of a fridge carries a large current.
items.why: False. On a normal day it carries nothing. It carries current only when a fault makes the metal body live.

items.p: A wall socket in India pushes with ____ volts.
items.why: India's mains supply is 230 volts. One AA cell is 1.5 volts.

items.p: Dry skin has a resistance of 100,000 ohms. Wet skin has 1,000 ohms. How many times easier is wet skin to pass?
items.why: 100,000 divided by 1,000 is 100. The same push sends about 100 times more current through the wet skin.

items.p: Three of these carry current using ions. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: sea water
lemon juice
a copper wire
a nerve in your arm
items.why: A copper wire carries current with free electrons. Sea water, lemon juice and a nerve all carry it with ions moving through water.

items.p: Sort each one by what carries the current inside it.
items.why: Metals and graphite have free electrons. Watery things, living or not, carry current with dissolved ions.

items.p: Put these in order, from the gentlest push to the hardest.
items: two AA cells in a row
a: two AA cells in a row
items.why: One cell is 1.5 volts and two in a row are 3 volts. A wall socket is 230 volts. Lightning is many millions of volts.

items.p: A wet grinder has a metal body and a plug with only two pins. Explain what could go wrong.
items.a: A two-pin plug has no earth pin, so the metal body is not joined to the ground. If a wire inside comes loose or gets wet and touches the body, the body becomes live. A person who touches it becomes the path to the ground.
items.why: A strong answer says what the missing pin was for, and names the person as the path the current takes when there is no easier one.

items.p: A torch bulb stays dark in salt water. An LED glows. Is salt water a conductor? Give your view and your reason.
items.a: A good answer takes a view and backs it. For example: it conducts, but far less well than a metal, so it gives enough current for an LED and too little for a bulb. Or: the question needs a number, not a yes or no.
items.why: There is no single right sentence. A strong answer notices that the answer depends on the tester, and that conducting comes in amounts.

items.p: Draw the path of a fault current in a mixer with an earth wire. Then draw it in a mixer without one.
items.a: First drawing: an arrow from the loose wire to the metal body, along the earth wire, into the ground. Second drawing: an arrow from the body through a person's hand and feet into the ground.
items.why: A strong pair of drawings shows that the current reaches the ground either way. The earth wire only changes whose path it is.

items.p: Three people disagree about what children should be told about water and electricity.

views.who: Meenakshi, a safety officer at an electricity board
views.says: Tell every child that water conducts. It is short, it is easy to remember, and short rules save lives.
Tell the truth. Pure water hardly conducts, and the ions do the carrying. A child who knows why will be careful in new places too.

views.who: Thangam, a grandmother who brought up four children
views.says: Give the rule and the reason on the same day. A rule alone gets broken, and a reason alone gets forgotten at the wrong moment.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and gives a reason from this lesson, such as: all everyday water has ions, or knowing about ions explains sweat and wet floors. It also gives one fair point to another view.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The short rule is safe and slightly untrue. The full truth is exact and takes longer to learn. Each speaker is protecting something real.

items.p: Why may a phone charger have only two pins and no earth pin?
opts: Its whole case is plastic, with no metal to touch
Chargers use no current
Phones are too small to be dangerous
items.why: An earth wire protects against a metal body going live. A charger wrapped fully in plastic has no metal body to protect. It still carries 230 volts inside, so a cracked charger is not safe.

items.p: Here are a wire and a nerve fibre, side by side. Label the conductor and the insulator in each.
a: the copper strands: conductor in the wire
the plastic coat: insulator on the wire
the salty water inside the fibre: conductor in the nerve
the fatty wrap called myelin: insulator on the nerve
items.why: Both are a conductor inside an insulating wrap. The wire uses free electrons in copper. The nerve uses ions in salty water, wrapped in fat.
items.art: A cut-open electric wire above a cut-open nerve fibre drawn to look alike: a core, a wrap round the core, and four blank label boxes joined by lines to the two cores and the two wraps.

items.p: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Why does only graphite conduct?
opts: Graphite is softer
Each atom in graphite has one electron free to move
Diamond is too clear
items.why: In diamond every outer electron is locked in a bond. In graphite the atoms sit in flat sheets, and one electron from each atom can move along the sheet. The atoms are the same. The joining is different.

items.p: What happens to air when lightning passes through it?
opts: The air turns into metal
Nothing. Lightning goes round the air
A huge push tears electrons free, so the air conducts
items.why: Air insulates until the push is about 30,000 volts for each centimetre. Beyond that, electrons are pulled off the air's atoms and the air carries a current for a moment.

items.p: Electricity takes only the easiest path, and none goes down any other path.
items.why: False. Current shares itself among every path open to it. The easier path gets more, but a harder path, such as a person, still gets some.

items.p: The purest water that can be made conducts nothing at all.
items.why: False. Kohlrausch and Heydweiller measured this in 1894. A few water molecules always split into ions by themselves, so even the purest water conducts a very little.

items.p: A material that has no resistance at all when it is cold enough is called a ____.
items.why: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes and his team found the first one in 1911, when they cooled mercury to minus 269 degrees Celsius.

items.p: Air starts to conduct at about 30,000 volts for each centimetre. About how many volts make a 3 centimetre spark?
items.why: 30,000 times 3 is 90,000 volts. That is why sparks from a socket are short, and why lightning needs many millions of volts.

items.p: Match each finding to the person who made it.
pairs: salts split into ions in water, 1884
resistance vanishes in very cold mercury, 1911
a crystal detector for radio waves, 1901
items.why: Gray was a cloth dyer. Arrhenius's examiners gave his idea of ions the lowest pass mark, and it later won a Nobel Prize. Bose worked in Kolkata with equipment he built himself.

items.p: Three of these are made from semiconductors. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: a solar panel
an LED
a copper wire
a computer chip
items.why: Copper is a metal and always conducts well. Solar panels, LEDs and chips are made of semiconductors, whose conducting can be controlled.

items.p: Put these findings in order, from the earliest to the latest.
items.why: Gilbert wrote in 1600. Gray's thread was 1729. Mercury was found to superconduct in 1911, and the ceramics in 1986.

items.p: Glass insulates when cold and conducts when red-hot. What does this tell you about the words conductor and insulator?
items.a: A good answer says that the words describe how a material behaves under certain conditions, not a fixed nature. The same glass gives a different answer when heat frees its charges.
items.why: A strong answer separates what a thing is made of from how it behaves, and names the condition that changed.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether rainwater or tap water conducts better. Say what you keep the same.
items.a: Use the LED tester on equal amounts of each water in equal clean plastic cups. Keep the same wire ends, the same gap and depth, the same cells and the same dim room. Rinse the wires between cups. Dip three times in each and compare the glow.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the water, repeats each test, and says how the result will be read. Catching the rain in clean plastic matters, because a metal bowl adds ions.

items.p: Draw one long scale from best conductor to best insulator. Place eight things on it.
items.a: A line with metals such as copper at one end, then pencil lead, salt water, tap water, wet wood or skin, and dry wood, plastic, rubber or glass at the far end.
items.why: A strong scale has metals at one end, insulators at the other, and at least three things placed in between. The exact order of near neighbours matters less than having a middle.

items.p: Scientists disagree about what the electric signals in plants mean.

views.says: Plants pass electric signals from cell to cell, weigh them and choose what to do. That is a kind of thinking, and we should study it as such.

views.who: Amedeo Alpi and 35 other plant scientists
views.says: The signals are real, but they do not run through nerve cells. Words like nerve and mind mislead. Call it signalling and growth.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give a reason. What test might help decide between them?
items.a: A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and suggests something to test, such as whether a plant acts differently after the same signal on different days, or whether blocking the signal changes what she does.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this. Both sides accept the measurements. They differ on what counts as thinking, and that is partly a question about words and partly one for more experiments.

items.p: A tester's lamp stays dark on a wooden block. What can you safely say?
opts: No charge can ever move in the block
Any current was too small for this lamp
The block is a perfect insulator
items.why: A dark lamp shows only that the current was below what the lamp needs. A more sensitive tester, a harder push or a wet block could give a different result.

items.p: Here is a power-line tower. Label the conductor and the three things that keep the current in it.
a: the long cable: bare aluminium wire
the stack between cable and tower: ceramic discs
the space all round the cable: air
items.why: The wire is bare because the air around it is the insulator. The ceramic discs hold the wire away from the steel tower, which is a conductor joined to the ground.
items.art: A tall steel power-line tower with one cable hanging from a stack of discs, with four blank label boxes joined by lines to the cable, the discs, the open air beside the cable and the tower frame.

applications: Covering every copper wire in plastic, so current reaches the fan and not the hand.
Earthing the metal body of a fridge, an iron or a wet grinder through the third pin of the plug.
Holding bare power lines away from steel towers with stacks of ceramic or glass discs.
Giving line workers rubber gloves, rubber mats and tools with insulated handles.
Checking drinking water with a small meter that measures how well the water conducts.
Making phone screens that sense the touch of a conducting fingertip.
Building computer chips and solar panels from silicon, a semiconductor whose conducting can be controlled.
Running the strong magnets of hospital MRI scanners with superconducting wire.
Fitting a copper strip from the top of a tall building to the ground, to lead lightning safely down.
Making tank alarms in which rising water joins two metal points and sounds a buzzer.

open_questions.q: How do the ceramic superconductors work?
open_questions.why_open: They were found in 1986. Thousands of experiments later, physicists still argue about what joins the electrons into pairs in them, and no theory has predicted the next material correctly.

open_questions.q: Can any material superconduct at room temperature without being squeezed?
open_questions.why_open: No law of nature is known to forbid it, but nobody has made one. Each claim so far has failed when other laboratories tried to repeat it.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do ions push past each other in crowded sea water?
open_questions.why_open: The simple rules work for weak salt water. In strong salt water the ions crowd and pull on each other, and chemists still cannot work out the conducting exactly from first rules.

open_questions.q: How much do plants, fungi and single cells use electric signals to remember and decide?
open_questions.why_open: The signals are real and measured. What they mean to the plant is hard to test, and scientists disagree on which words are honest to use.

open_questions.q: How do the electric signals in a brain become a feeling, such as the sting of a small static shock?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow ions through nerve gates in great detail. Nobody has yet shown how any amount of moving charge becomes the feeling itself.

maths.problem: In the Water Test, the five cups scored 0, 1, 0, 2 and 3 for glow. Draw a bar chart of the scores. Which two cups have equal bars, and what does that tell you?
maths.answer: Cups A and C both score 0. Plain water and sugar water conduct the same, so sugar added nothing that carries current.
maths.explain: Draw five bars with heights 0, 1, 0, 2 and 3. A bar of height 0 is still a result. Equal bars for A and C show that dissolving sugar changed nothing.
maths.context: This is about showing the glow scores from the Water Test as a picture.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets you see at a glance which cups are alike and which stand apart.

maths.problem: You tested 12 things. 4 lit the bulb. 3 lit only the LED. The rest lit neither. What fraction lit neither? What fraction let some current through?
maths.answer: 5 out of 12 lit neither. 7 out of 12 let some current through.
maths.explain: 12 minus 4 minus 3 is 5, so 5 twelfths lit neither. 4 plus 3 is 7, so 7 twelfths let some current through.
maths.context: This is about counting the results of the Two Testers experiment.
maths.why_maths: Fractions show how the answer to 'how many conduct?' changes when you change the tester.

maths.problem: One AA cell pushes with 1.5 volts. How many AA cells in a row would you need to push at least as hard as a 230 volt socket?
maths.explain: 153 cells give 153 times 1.5, which is 229.5 volts, just short. 154 cells give 231 volts. So you need 154.
maths.context: This is about how much harder the mains pushes than a cell.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows the size of the gap between a safe push and a deadly one, as a number you can picture.

maths.problem: Sea water conducts about 1,000,000 times better than the purest water. Tap water conducts about 100 times worse than sea water. About how many times better than the purest water does tap water conduct?
maths.explain: 1,000,000 divided by 100 is 10,000. So tap water sits between the two, much nearer to sea water than a bulb tester suggests.
maths.context: This is about placing three kinds of water on the long scale of conducting.
maths.why_maths: Scaling by tens, hundreds and thousands is the only way to compare things as far apart as conductors and insulators.

maths.problem: Lakshmi says: if the bulb lights, the thing is a conductor. Her bulb did not light on a tomato. She says: so the tomato is an insulator. Is her reasoning sound?
maths.answer: No. Her rule says what follows when the bulb lights. It says nothing about what follows when the bulb stays dark.
maths.explain: From 'if the bulb lights, it conducts' you cannot turn the rule round. A thing may conduct too little to light a bulb. The LED showed that the tomato does.
maths.context: This is about what a dark bulb does and does not prove.
maths.why_maths: If-then logic shows exactly why a test that finds nothing has not proved there is nothing.

roots.context: You have asked water, a pencil, a tomato and your own fingertip the same question with two testers, and the testers did not always agree. Now we ask what that says about the boxes we sort the world into, and about where you end.

deep_truth.truth: In the Water Test, the torch bulb stayed dark in salt water and the LED glowed. One tester said insulator and the other said conductor, about the same cup. The water had not changed. So conductor and insulator are not two kinds of matter. They are two answers, and the answer depends on how hard we push and how closely we look.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into pairs of boxes, conductor or insulator, safe or dangerous, me or not me, and then treat the boxes as if nature had made them. This lesson's testers show the boxes were made by the question we asked.
deep_truth.evidence: The same salt water left a bulb dark and lit an LED. Each pinch of salt raised the glow by a step, with no jump. Dry paper was dark and the same paper wet was not. Air insulates until the push reaches 30,000 volts for each centimetre.

three.who_am_i: You are salty water inside a thin skin. The skin holds back a small push and gives way to a large one. Every nerve in you is a conductor wrapped in a fatty insulator, carrying signals as moving ions. So your edge is not one fixed wall. Whether a thing is outside you or passing through you depends on what is pushing.
three.what_is_life: Every living cell is conducting water inside an insulating coat with tiny gates in it. A cell lives by choosing, moment by moment, which ions may cross. A touch-me-not plant, a shark and a bumblebee all send or sense electric signals. Life did not wait for wires. Life is made of conductors and insulators that open and close.
three.what_is_this_world: The same carbon atoms make diamond, which insulates, and graphite, which conducts. The same air insulates all day and conducts for one moment as lightning. Charge is in everything. Whether the charge moves depends on how the atoms are joined, and on the push, the heat and the wetness. The world is not divided into the stuff that carries and the stuff that blocks.

roots.thread: Every material is full of charge. In some the charge is free, in some it is held, and in most it is held only up to a point. A cell, a socket and a thundercloud are three sizes of the same push, and a material that says no to one may say yes to the next. So the two words in the title of this lesson describe a meeting between a material and a push, not a material alone. Consciousness is the ground from which all of this arises: the copper and the plastic, the push and the one who is pushed. From that ground, the line between what conducts and what does not is one of many lines that thought draws for its own use.

teachings.teaching: It moves, and it does not move. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
teachings.link: The sages who composed this verse refused to put the deepest reality into one box of a pair. The salt water in your cup would not go into one box either: it conducted for the LED and did not conduct for the bulb.

teachings.teaching: Knowledge is gained through the means of knowing and through standpoints. The Jain teachers built on this to say that every statement about a thing is true from some standpoint, and should be said with the words 'in some respect'.
teachings.link: In some respect salt water is a conductor, and in some respect it is not. The bulb and the LED are two standpoints. A Jain teacher would say that neither tester lied, and neither told the whole of it.

teachings.teaching: Everything can be called 'that', and everything can be called 'this'. 'That' comes out of 'this', and 'this' depends on 'that'. The sage does not go by such divisions, and sees things in the light of the whole.
teachings.link: Zhuangzi, writing in China about 2,300 years ago, taught that the two sides of any division are made together. We could not have named insulators without conductors, and the pencil and the tomato sit on the line between.

science.text: Materials differ in how easily charge moves through them along one unbroken scale covering more than twenty powers of ten. Where the words conductor and insulator divide that scale is a human choice.
Whether a material conducts depends on the push, the temperature, light, water and purity. Air, glass and silicon each change from insulating to conducting.
Cells of every kind, not only nerves, may use patterns of voltage to remember and decide. Michael Levin's experiments support this, and many biologists read them differently.
How moving ions in a brain become a felt experience is not known.

other_view.who: The Vaisheshika school of Kanada, and many physicists and engineers today
other_view.view: Qualities really belong to substances. Copper has a conductivity that can be measured to many figures, and it is the same in every laboratory on Earth. The difference between copper and rubber is as real as anything in nature. That our lamps have thresholds says something about lamps, and nothing deep about the world or about the self. The boxes are rough, but what they point to was not made up by us.

practice.title: The edge of the hand
practice.say: Sit and rest one hand on a steel tumbler and the other on a wooden table. Close your eyes. Notice that the steel seems cold and the wood seems warm, though both are as warm as the room. The steel is carrying your warmth away, and the wood is not. Breathe slowly five times. With each breath, ask where your hand ends and the tumbler begins.
practice.kid: Put one hand on steel and one on wood. Close your eyes. Which seems colder? Breathe slowly five times. Where does your hand end?

ask: The bulb and the LED gave different answers about the same water. Was one of them wrong, or were they answering different questions?
A small push stops at your skin and a large push goes through. So is your skin the edge of you?
Can you think of any two boxes that have nothing at all in between them?
If the boxes come from our questions, what was there before anyone asked?

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home, so the glow scores are what the physics predicts. The Water Test: a red LED on two fresh AA cells should show nothing or almost nothing in filtered water, a faint glow in tap water, the same as plain in sugar water, a clear glow with lemon and a bright glow with salt. The size of the glow depends on the wire ends, the gap and the local tap water. Steel paper clips or bare copper ends both dissolve a little, which helps the current. The steps say what to do if nothing glows, up to adding a third cell. The LED must be red: white and blue LEDs need more push than two cells give through water. Touching the two ends together for more than a moment can burn out an LED on two AA cells, so the steps say one second only, bulb first on solids, and a spare LED. Two Testers: a whole pencil may leave the bulb dim or dark depending on its grade, and both results teach the same point. A fingertip at 3 volts is harmless. The Full Bucket Signal gives only a faint glow with thin wire ends in tap water, and that is used as the starting problem. Facts to check before this lesson goes live: Desaguliers and the date of the two names (1742), Gray's 765 feet (1729), the Kohlrausch and Heydweiller measurement (1894), Bose's galena detector (made 1901, American patent 755,840 granted 1904), the File and Mills persistent current (1963), the lanthanum hydride results (2019), Alpi and others (2007, 36 authors), Clarke and others on bumblebees (2013), Durant and others on flatworms (2017), the body resistance figures (100,000 ohms dry, 1,000 ohms wet), and the three museum addresses.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time people sorted materials by rubbing. In 1600 William Gilbert, a doctor in London, listed the things that pulled dust and straw after rubbing: amber, glass, wax. He called them electrics. Metals did nothing when rubbed, so people believed metals had no electricity in them. In 1729 Stephen Gray, a cloth dyer living on charity in London, rubbed a glass tube and found that the pull travelled along a damp hemp thread. With his friend Granville Wheler he sent it 765 feet across a garden. It worked only when the thread hung from silk. When they hung it from brass wire, the pull was lost. So the metal had carried it away. Metals were the best carriers of all. They had never held a charge when rubbed only because it ran off through the hand. In 1733 Charles du Fay in Paris charged metal, and himself, while hanging from silk cords. By 1742 John Desaguliers had given the two kinds their names: conductors and insulators.
how_we_found_out.who: William Gilbert, Stephen Gray and Granville Wheler in England, Charles du Fay in Paris, and John Desaguliers in London
how_we_found_out.when: 1600 (Gilbert's list), 1729 (Gray's thread), 1733 (du Fay) and 1742 (the two names)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that metals had no electricity in them, because a rubbed metal rod pulled nothing. Gray's thread showed the opposite. Metals carry electricity so well that the charge had been running away through the hand that held them.
how_we_found_out.context: Who first sorted materials into conductors and insulators? This card tells how a dyer with a thread overturned a list that had stood for more than a hundred years.

quiz: Every material has electric charges inside it.
All atoms hold charges. In a conductor some are free to move, and in an insulator they are held.
Sugar water conducts as well as salt water.
Sugar stays as whole molecules with no charge. Salt breaks into ions, which carry current.
The current in salt water is carried by ions.
Plus ions and minus ions drift in opposite directions between the two wires.
A dark bulb proves that no current at all is flowing.
It shows only that the current is too small for that bulb. An LED may still glow.
Pencil lead conducts electricity.
The lead is graphite, a form of carbon with one free electron on each atom.
The earth wire carries current all day long.
It carries current only when a fault makes the metal body of an appliance live.
Air can conduct when the push is large enough.
At about 30,000 volts for each centimetre, air gives way. That is a spark, or lightning.
Rubber chappals make it safe to touch a live wire.
A thin, wet or dirty sole is not made or tested for 230 volts.
Wet skin lets more current through than dry skin.
Wet skin is about 100 times easier for a current to pass.
The purest water conducts nothing at all.
A few water molecules always split into ions, so even the purest water conducts a very little.
odd: The first three are metals with free electrons, but plastic holds every electron in place.
The first three hold many ions, but sugar dissolves without making any.
The first three are insulators that keep fingers from live metal, but a pin is a conductor.
The first three are made from semiconductors, but an iron nail is a plain metal conductor.
The first three make a home safer, but a wet floor gives current an easy path.
